words.definition: To treat or describe something as far less important than it really is.
words.example: Don't trivialize her injury; that sprained ankle could take weeks to heal.
words.mnemonic: trivia + -ize: to turn a serious matter into mere 'trivia,' a small throwaway fact.

words.definition: To state support for or belief in something again, with renewed conviction.
words.example: After the scandal, the mayor reaffirmed her commitment to open government.
words.mnemonic: re- (again) + affirm (declare true) = to declare it true all over again.

words.definition: Tending to expect the worst possible outcome in any situation.
words.example: He was so pessimistic about the road trip that he packed for a breakdown.
words.mnemonic: Starts like 'pest' — a pest always assumes the gloomiest ending.

words.definition: Hopeful and confident that good things are likely to happen.
words.example: Even after three rejections, she stayed optimistic about the next interview.
words.mnemonic: 'opt' for the best — you are choosing to see the bright side.

words.definition: Confident and direct in expressing one's needs, views, or boundaries.
words.example: Her assertive tone in the meeting made everyone stop and listen.
words.mnemonic: From 'assert' — an assertive person firmly asserts what they want.

words.definition: Having plenty of money and a comfortable, high standard of living.
words.example: They moved to an affluent suburb with manicured lawns and private schools.
words.mnemonic: 'a-fluent' — money flows (fluent = flowing) freely toward you.

words.definition: Showing great riches through a grand and luxurious display.
words.example: The opulent ballroom dripped with gold chandeliers and deep velvet drapes.
words.mnemonic: 'opu' sounds like 'opal' — a glittering jewel; opulent means jewel-rich.

words.definition: Given or spent in very large, generous, and often excessive amounts.
words.example: He threw a lavish party with imported caviar and a live orchestra.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'lather' — you lather it on thick and generously.

words.definition: Spending or costing much more than is necessary or reasonable.
words.example: Her extravagant shopping sprees left every credit card maxed out.
words.mnemonic: extra- + vag (wander): spending that wanders way past sensible limits.

words.definition: Splendid and clearly very costly, suggesting rich indulgence.
words.example: The hotel served a sumptuous feast of lobster, truffles, and aged wine.
words.mnemonic: Think 'consume' — a sumptuous spread is made for grand consuming.

words.definition: Lacking money, food, and the basic means of survival.
words.example: After the factory closed, many families were left destitute and homeless.
words.mnemonic: 'de-stitute' — stripped of (de-) everything you were set up with.

words.definition: Reduced to a state of having very little money or resources.
words.example: The long war left the once-prosperous region impoverished and struggling.
words.mnemonic: im- (to make) + Latin 'pauper' (a poor person) = made into a pauper.

words.definition: The condition of being extremely short of money and basic goods.
words.example: Growing up in poverty, she wore hand-me-downs and often skipped meals.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'pauper' — a pauper's life defines this state of want.

words.definition: So short of money as to lack the basic necessities of life.
words.example: The clinic offers free care to indigent patients who cannot pay.
words.mnemonic: 'in-dig' — having to dig through scraps because you own nothing.

words.definition: A severe and grinding lack of money; extreme want.
words.example: The once-famous actor spent his final years in penury, selling off his awards.
words.mnemonic: 'penny-ury' — down to your very last penny.

words.definition: The state of not having something considered a basic necessity.
words.example: Sleep deprivation left her unable to focus during the long afternoon meeting.
words.mnemonic: From 'de-' (away) + 'private' — something basic and private is taken away from you.

words.definition: A special advantage or right available only to a particular person or group.
words.example: Members enjoy the privilege of entering the lounge before the general public.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'privus' (private) + 'lex' (law): a private law written just for you.

words.definition: The belief that one inherently deserves special treatment, rights, or rewards.
words.example: His sense of entitlement meant he expected a promotion without ever earning it.
words.mnemonic: Picture someone clutching a 'title' deed, insisting they own every advantage.

words.definition: Using money and resources carefully and without waste.
words.example: Being thrifty, she compared prices at three stores before buying a single item.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'thrive + fifty' — you thrive by saving every fifty cents.

words.definition: Extremely unwilling to spend or share money.
words.example: The miserly landlord refused to fix the heating just to save a few dollars.
words.mnemonic: Contains 'miser' — a miser makes everyone around him MISERable guarding his coins.

words.definition: Excessively careful or stingy with money and resources.
words.example: The parsimonious manager rationed paper clips as if they were made of gold.
words.mnemonic: 'Parse your money' so finely that you split every single penny.

words.definition: Extreme greed for wealth or material gain.
words.example: His avarice drove him to cheat lifelong friends out of their savings.
words.mnemonic: A-VARICE: imagine 'a vise' gripping a pile of money and never letting go.

words.definition: Strongly desiring to gain and possess more things or wealth.
words.example: Her acquisitive nature filled the house with gadgets she never actually used.
words.mnemonic: Built on 'acquire' — an acquisitive person always itches to acquire more.

words.definition: A focus on owning possessions and physical comforts over spiritual values.
words.example: The film criticized suburban materialism, where happiness meant owning a bigger car.
words.mnemonic: Think 'material' (stuff) + '-ism' — a whole belief system built around owning stuff.

words.definition: To gather and store a large supply, often secretly.
words.example: During the shortage, people began to hoard toilet paper and canned goods.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'horde' — you stash away a whole horde of goods in your closet.

words.definition: A very large quantity of something; more than enough.
words.example: The harvest brought an abundance of apples, far more than the family could eat.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'a bundle' inside it — bundles upon bundles, overflowing everywhere.

words.definition: An unexpected gain of money or good fortune.
words.example: The surprise inheritance was a windfall that let them pay off the house early.
words.mnemonic: Fruit the WIND blew FALLing off the tree — free riches you didn't work for.

words.definition: A society or system governed by its richest people.
words.example: Critics called the nation a plutocracy, quietly run by a handful of billionaires.
words.mnemonic: 'Pluto' (Roman god of underground riches) + '-cracy' (rule): rule by the rich.

words.definition: To use someone or something unfairly for your own benefit.
words.example: The factory was accused of exploiting workers with brutal hours and low pay.
words.mnemonic: Read it as 'ex + ploy' — a ploy to squeeze out every drop of advantage.

words.definition: A lack of fairness or justice in how things are distributed.
words.example: The report exposed the inequity between executive bonuses and frontline workers' wages.
words.mnemonic: 'In-' (not) + 'equity' (fairness) = not fair; don't confuse it with 'iniquity' (sin).

words.definition: The condition of having plenty of money and a high standard of living.
words.example: Their gated mansion and three cars signaled the affluence of the neighborhood.
words.mnemonic: Say it 'a-FLU-ence' — money flows toward you like a flood.

words.definition: A state of filth, misery, and neglect, usually caused by extreme poverty.
words.example: The tenants lived in squalor, crammed into damp rooms with no running water.
words.mnemonic: 'Squalor' blends 'squalid' + 'horror' — the horror of a grimy, wretched place.

words.definition: To leave money or possessions to another person through a will after death.
words.example: In her will, the widow chose to bequeath her grand piano to her granddaughter.
words.mnemonic: 'Be-QUEATH' → picture a queen who, before she goes, hands down her jewels.

words.definition: Money or property received from a person after they have died.
words.example: He used the inheritance from his late uncle to buy a small farm.
words.mnemonic: An 'heir' sits right in the middle of in-HEIR-itance — what heirs collect.

words.definition: A rich and influential person, especially a leader in business or industry.
words.example: The oil magnate owned refineries on three continents and flew in a private jet.
words.mnemonic: 'Magnate' sounds like 'magnet' — a tycoon who pulls in money and power.

words.definition: The most powerful, wealthy, or talented members of a group or society.
words.example: Only the elite could afford tickets to the exclusive charity gala.
words.mnemonic: 'E-LITE' — the chosen few who are 'lit,' seated at the very top.

words.definition: The highest class in society, typically people born into noble, titled families.
words.example: Members of the aristocracy arrived at the ball in tiaras and inherited jewels.
words.mnemonic: From Greek 'aristos' (best) + 'cracy' (rule) — rule by the best-born.

words.definition: Affecting a whole body, structure, or society rather than just one part.
words.example: The report exposed systemic corruption running through every branch of the government.
words.mnemonic: Think of it spreading through the entire system, like blood moving through the body.

words.definition: Spreading widely and without control, usually something harmful.
words.example: Inflation was rampant, and prices nearly doubled within a single year.
words.mnemonic: 'Rampant' → problems race up the 'ramp,' speeding out of control.

words.definition: To share something out again, dividing it differently among people or places.
words.example: The new tax policy aimed to redistribute wealth from the rich to the poor.
words.mnemonic: 'Re-' (again) + distribute — to divide and hand things out once more.

words.definition: To set aside or assign a resource for a particular purpose or person.
words.example: The manager decided to allocate half the budget to marketing this quarter.
words.mnemonic: 'A-LOCATE' — you find a location or slot for each resource.

words.definition: To officially impose or collect a tax, fee, or fine.
words.example: The council voted to levy a new charge on every plastic bag sold.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'levare,' to lift — the government lifts money straight out of your pocket.

words.definition: To help pay for something with money, usually from a government or organization.
words.example: The state agreed to subsidize farmers so that bread would stay cheap.
words.mnemonic: 'Sub' (under) + sit — the money sits underneath to prop up the cost.

words.definition: Existing in large amounts; giving generously and in great plenty.
words.example: After the rains, the harvest was bountiful and the barns overflowed with grain.
words.mnemonic: Hidden inside is 'bounty' — a huge reward, full to the brim.

words.definition: Using humor, irony, or exaggeration to criticize people or society.
words.example: The satirical cartoon mocked the mayor by drawing him as a greedy, bloated clown.
words.mnemonic: Picture a late-night comedy 'sat' down to write jokes that skewer politicians.

words.definition: Happening in a way opposite to what you expect, often with a wry twist.
words.example: It was ironic that the fire station burned down while the crew was out fighting another blaze.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'iron-ick' — imagine an iron that refuses to press wrinkles and instead adds them, the exact opposite of its job.

words.definition: To give a false impression of something, or to contradict and disprove it.
words.example: Her calm voice belied the panic she felt as the plane dropped through the storm.
words.mnemonic: Break it into 'be-lie' — to make something 'be a lie', hiding the truth behind a false surface.

words.definition: Producing a great deal of money or profit.
words.example: She quit teaching for a lucrative consulting job that doubled her salary within a year.
words.mnemonic: Think of 'loot' hidden in 'lucr-' (Latin lucrum, gain) — a lucrative deal fills your bag with loot.
